E1781.summary: The Tree of Life: its attainment is laborious intellectual work (Van Helmont), and for Atwood it lies hidden and hard to find under the oblivion of natural birth.
E1781.body: Van Helmont, as quoted, says that “the attainment of the Tree of Life is laborious, and the fruit of intellectual research” [III.1 ¶13]. Atwood herself writes that “The tree of life covered over, indeed, with the dark oblivion of this natural outbirth, is latent and difficult to find” [III.1 ¶34]. According to the reader's record, she adds there that it is revealed only by celestial instinct, and that its bough, not the whole tree, is to be taken.

E1782.summary: Trevisan (Trevisanus), cited by Atwood for long, fruitless labour before success and for his image of the fixed watery Form as a marvellous fountain.
E1782.body: Atwood cites Trevisan as an example of one who worked in vain for over half a century until he found the separated Light [III.1 ¶37]. She also names him alongside Artefius [IV.3 ¶7]. In the footnotes, Trevisanus (spelled there “Berhard Trevisan”) is cited from his *Opusculum*. Atwood uses him to illustrate the fixed watery Form, his marvellous fountain, “shining like silver and of caerulean clearness” [I.3 n38, I.3 n39].

E1783.summary: In the quoted Chaldaic oracle, the threefold that shines throughout the world under the Monad's rule, in which Virtue, Wisdom and Verity appear.
E1783.body: The voice here is the Chaldaic oracle, quoted by Atwood: “For in the whole world shineth the Triad over which the Monad rules.” [IV.2 ¶22]. The oracle goes on: “And there appeared in it (the triad) Virtue, Wisdom, and multscient Verity;” [IV.2 ¶24]. The reader's record adds that all things serve its three Principles.

E1784.summary: A threefold turning inward which, together with multiplication of the hypostatic unit, makes the magistery manifest.
E1784.body: Atwood says the magistery is “made manifest by a triple introversion and multiplication of the hypostatic unit” [IV.2 ¶37]. The text does not explain the expression further. Reading it as a threefold turning inward follows the wording and is not a definition the book gives.

E1785.summary: Triptolemus appears only in a simile: Hippocrates spread Aesculapius's remedies as Triptolemus spread the seed of Ceres.
E1785.body: Atwood's only use of Triptolemus is in a simile. Hippocrates dispersed the succours of Aesculapius as Triptolemus dispersed the seed of Ceres [IV.3 ¶32].

E1786.summary: Grinding, used figuratively for the continual, slow and gentle working of the Philosophic Subject, which dissolves the subject's innate defects.
E1786.body: Atwood uses the word figuratively, marking it with “as it were”. The aim is “by a continual mechanic trituration, as it were, to dissolve and ultimately obliterate its innate defects” [IV.1 ¶5]. She applies the point “especially to the trituration of the Philosophic Subject” [IV.1 ¶13]. The record for that passage says this working should be slow, gentle and continuous. The context suggests that the word stands for the continual working of the subject, not for literal grinding.

E1788.summary: In the Appendix, Atwood's term for Theosophy on its physical side, as opposed to the alchemy the world has sought without finding.
E1788.body: This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer. Atwood says: “True Alchemy (not that which the world has run after without finding) is related to Theosophy on its physical side” [APP ¶78]. According to the reader's record, she describes it there as a change in the circulatory system of the blood wrought by reiterative contritions.

E1790.summary: The Platonists, as Atwood reports, declared true Being to be white.
E1790.body: Atwood reports a view of the Platonists: “The Platonists have declared true Being to be white” [III.2 ¶9].

E1791.summary: The genuine art, as distinct from “clouds of sophistry”, whose Light and virtue helped the ancients.
E1791.body: Atwood speaks of “that Light and virtue of true Chemistry, by which the ancients were assisted” [III.1 ¶4]. The reader's record says she sets this genuine art apart from clouds of sophistry.

E1792.summary: In Aliphili's words, an essence produced in man by conjoining the elements, which alone dissolves gold into black earth; called the great and miraculous mystery of the world.
E1792.body: The voice here is Aliphili, as quoted. The reader's record gives his account: an essence produced in man by conjoining the elements, which dissolves gold into black earth, and nothing else does this. Aliphili names it “the great and miraculous mystery of the world; that is the true fiery water” [II.1 ¶14]. This gives the identity: true fiery water = the great and miraculous mystery of the world [II.1 ¶14].

E1793.summary: The real object of Alchemy's golden promise; avarice, ambition and curiosity cannot reach it, and only Reason enters it.
E1793.body: Atwood contrasts the true Form of Gold with the dead metal: “neither will be found to be the true Form of Gold” [III.4 ¶11]. According to the reader's record, she makes it the real object of Alchemy's golden promise there. Avarice, ambition and curiosity cannot reach it, and only Reason enters it. The text does not define it further here.

E1794.summary: Apparently the real being or substance of oneself, which self-contemplation with an unpurified spirit cannot discern.
E1794.body: Atwood warns that if we contemplate ourselves with an unpurified spirit, “we shall not there discern the true hypostasis” [II.2 ¶14]. The reading as the real being or substance of oneself is inferred from this context, not stated.

E1795.summary: The identity in nature that the pseudo-alchemists failed to divine, which would otherwise have to be sought through all creatures by experiment.
E1795.body: Atwood says the pseudo-alchemists worked “without rightly divining the true Identity of nature” [II.1 ¶6]. Without the one subject that contains all, one would have “to search out the identity through all creatures and minerals, by way of experiment” [II.1 ¶9].

E1796.summary: The proper object of intellectual inquiry in itself, which the wise mind holds within itself; the intellect receives it and becomes one with it.
E1796.body: Atwood glosses the term herself: “(since it possesses the true Intelligible); that is to say, the proper object of intellectual inquiry in itself” [II.1 ¶37]. This gives the identity: the true Intelligible = the proper object of intellectual inquiry in itself [II.1 ¶37]. According to the reader's record, the wise mind holds it within itself, and the intellect receives it and becomes one with it.

E1797.summary: That on whose discovery the success of the experiment depends; it is present more or less in every mind, though not clearly discernible in all.
E1797.body: Atwood says that success “depends on the discovery of the true Intention” [IV.3 ¶54]. According to the reader's record, she adds that it is involved more or less in every mind, though it cannot be clearly distinguished in all.

E1798.summary: In the Appendix, the mind's experimental contact with mystery, in which the mind consciously enters the Universal and knows itself in its principle.
E1798.body: This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer. Atwood says: “True Knowledge is experimental contact of mind with mystery” [APP ¶75]. According to the reader's record, the mind there consciously enters the Universal and knows itself in its principle, with an efflux of life.

E1799.summary: The Light needed before practice; hidden and imprisoned within, it is called the fountain of Universal Nature, and is perfected in the Saviour.
E1799.body:
Atwood uses the term in three passages.

- **Needed before practice.** Those who failed worked “without the true Light or heeding their injunctions” [I.1 ¶86]. It is not explained there.
- **Hidden within.** She speaks of “the true light shut up as in a prison, the fountain of Universal Nature” [II.1 ¶49]. This gives the identity: true light = the fountain of Universal Nature. According to the record, the senses' outward attraction keeps this light apart from understanding.
- **In the Saviour.** She quotes “The True Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world” [IV.2 ¶19]. According to the record, the Light is perfected in the Saviour, and one ray of it cleanses our life.

The text does not say outright that these three uses are one and the same.

E1800.summary: In Rabbi Ben Jochai's words, man as distinct from the man who appears here.
E1800.body: The voice here is Rabbi Ben Jochai, as quoted: “But we must distinguish the true man from him who is here apparent” [II.1 ¶42].

E1801.summary: The material and proper Subject of the Work, hidden under countless names; finding it is called a great point.
E1801.body: The passage says: “It is a great point to find out the True Matter and proper Subject of this work” [IV.2 ¶6]. This gives the identity: True Matter = proper Subject of this work. According to the reader's record, it is hidden under countless names and is not named here. The voice is unclear. It may be Atwood, or she may be continuing a cited author, since the next sentence reads “adds our author of The Triumph”.

E1802.summary: In the Paracelsians' view, a medicine bound in man like milk in a hard nut, which must be freed from impure envelopes to become pure crystalline matter.
E1802.body: Atwood reports the Paracelsian view: “The true medicine, according to the Paracelsians, is bound in man” [III.1 ¶10]. According to the reader's record, it is held there like milk in a hard nut. It must be freed from its impure envelopes to become pure crystalline matter.

E1803.summary: That which the Art restores to its original rule by hiding the opposing principle; not otherwise defined.
E1803.body: The Art is said to work “to restore the true rector to his original rule” [II.1 ¶21]. According to the reader's record, it does this by hiding the opposing principle. The voice is unclear, and the text does not define the term further.

E1804.summary: In the Appendix, the identity of knower and known, of subject with object.
E1804.body: This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer. Atwood says: “True Science is the contact identical of the thing knowing with the thing known, subject with object.” [APP ¶171]

E1805.summary: In Eirenaeus, the means by which the purged Mercury is vivified; not explained further.
E1805.body: The voice here is Eirenaeus, as quoted. Of the purged Mercury he says: “And with true sulfur it can vivify” [III.1 ¶69]. The text does not explain the term further.

E1806.summary: In Paracelsus, the matter of the metals, which brings everything into its due form.
E1806.body: The voice here is Paracelsus, as quoted: “The truphat, or matter of the metals” [I.2 ¶25]. This gives the identity: truphat = matter of the metals. According to the reader's record, it brings everything into its due form.

E1807.summary: In the Appendix, Light in its own ether: the Divine Wisdom made visible to itself.
E1807.body: This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer. Atwood says: “Truth is, as it were, Light in its own ether, the Divine Wisdom self-conspicuous” [APP ¶171]. This gives the identity: Truth = Divine Wisdom self-conspicuous.

E1808.summary: Atwood's name for the Chaldaic oracles (Oracula Chaldaica), which she cites on piety, the fiery mind, and the soul's way of return.
E1808.body: Atwood cites the truth-telling Oracle from the *Oracula Chaldaica* in II.3. She uses it in support of these points: piety and the fiery mind preserve the body; the soul's way of return; the warning against stooping down; and the soul clasping God. One line she quotes is “If thou extend the fiery mind to the work of piety,” [II.3 ¶37, II.3 ¶38, II.3 ¶40, II.3 ¶42, II.3 n46, II.3 n47]. She cites it with approval.

E1809.summary: The Turba, whose maxim that all the wise seek is in Mercury serves as a chapter epigraph and is taken up again in the text.
E1809.body: Atwood quotes the *Turba* (Ecercit. 1) as the epigraph of chapter I.2: “Est in Mercurio quicquid quaerunt Sapientes” [I.2 ¶1]. In modern English (our translation): whatever the Wise seek is in Mercury. She takes the maxim up again in [I.2 ¶12].

E1810.summary: In the theosophist's words, a heavenly and an earthly matter, to be reduced to one as they were at the beginning.
E1810.body: The voice here is the theosophist, as quoted: “That Two Natures be reduced to One, as they were at the beginning.” [IV.3 ¶38]. According to the reader's record, the two are a heavenly and an earthly matter.

E1811.summary: Two principles that stand against each other if the Chaos is split apart too early; not named here.
E1811.body: Atwood warns that if the Chaos is split apart too early, “the two Principles stand up one against the other, before the intended mastery is secure” [IV.1 ¶15]. She does not name the two Principles here.

E1812.summary: In Plato, as quoted, an ignorance that does not know it is ignorant and therefore has no desire to emerge.
E1812.body: The voice here is Plato, as quoted. He describes an ignorance “which being ignorant that it is ignorant has no desire to emerge” [II.2 ¶13].
